title: Life Processes
subject: science
syllabus_note: Follows the CBSE 2025-26 syllabus: 'living beings' and their basic concept of nutrition, respiration, transport and excretion in plants and animals.

blocks.title: Even when you sleep, you are busy
blocks.body:
When you sleep, you do not walk, talk or play. Yet you are alive. Inside you, food is being digested, air is moving in and out, blood is flowing and waste is being removed.

These **maintenance** jobs never stop, even at the level of molecules. They are called **life processes**: **nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion**. In this chapter you will see how plants and animals, including you, carry out each of them.

blocks.title: The man who found the cell's energy coin
blocks.body:
Yellapragada SubbaRow was born in Bhimavaram, Andhra Pradesh. At Harvard, with Cyrus Fiske, he discovered **phosphocreatine** and **ATP** in muscle: the molecule that every cell uses as its energy currency.

Later he led the teams that made **methotrexate**, a cancer medicine, and **aureomycin**, one of the first tetracycline antibiotics. Few people knew his name, but his work saved millions of lives.
blocks.future: Physiology and biochemistry lead to careers in medicine, nursing, pharmacy, nutrition, sports science, agriculture and biotechnology.

blocks.question: Why can a single-celled amoeba get oxygen by diffusion alone, but a human cannot?
options: Most human cells are far from the air, so diffusion is too slow
blocks.explanation: In a large body, most cells are not in contact with the air; diffusion over such distances is far too slow, so we need special organs for breathing and transport.

blocks.title: Autotrophs and heterotrophs
blocks.body:
- **Autotrophic nutrition:** the organism makes its own food from simple inorganic substances, carbon dioxide and water, using sunlight. Green plants and some bacteria are **autotrophs**.
- **Heterotrophic nutrition:** the organism takes in food made by others. Animals, fungi and most bacteria are **heterotrophs**. Some break food down outside the body (fungi such as bread mould), some take in whole food and break it down inside (amoeba, humans), and some feed on living hosts without killing them (**parasites** such as cuscuta, ticks, lice, leeches and tapeworms).

**Photosynthesis** has three events:
1. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
2. Light energy becomes chemical energy, and water is split into hydrogen and oxygen.
3. Carbon dioxide is reduced to carbohydrates.

In the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll: $\mathrm{6CO_{2} + 12H_{2}O \rightarrow C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} + 6O_{2} + 6H_{2}O}$

Plants take in carbon dioxide through **stomata**, tiny pores on the leaf. Each pore is opened and closed by two **guard cells**: they swell when water flows in, opening the pore, and shrink when they lose water, closing it. Water comes from the soil through the roots; nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and magnesium are taken up from the soil as minerals.

blocks.title: How amoeba and paramecium eat
blocks.body:
- **Amoeba** pushes out finger-like extensions of its cell surface (**pseudopodia**), which fuse around a food particle to form a **food vacuole**. Inside the vacuole, food is broken down and diffuses into the cytoplasm; the undigested remains are thrown out at the surface.
- **Paramecium** has a fixed shape, so food enters at a specific spot. Movements of the **cilia** covering its body sweep food to that spot.

blocks.question: A destarched potted plant is kept in the dark for a day. Which of these is it unable to do?
options: Take in water through its roots
blocks.explanation: Photosynthesis needs sunlight; in the dark the plant still absorbs water, respires and loses some water.
option_feedback: Some water is still lost from the leaves.
Correct!
Roots absorb water even in the dark.
Plants respire day and night.

blocks.title: The alimentary canal
blocks.body:
The **alimentary canal** is a long tube from the mouth to the anus. Food is pushed along it by rhythmic contraction of its muscles, called **peristalsis**.

1. **Mouth:** teeth crush the food; the tongue mixes it with saliva. **Salivary amylase** breaks starch into sugar.
2. **Oesophagus:** carries food to the stomach by peristalsis.
3. **Stomach:** gastric glands release **hydrochloric acid** (makes the medium acidic so that **pepsin** can act), pepsin (digests proteins) and **mucus** (protects the lining from the acid). A **sphincter** muscle lets food out a little at a time.
4. **Small intestine:** the longest part. **Bile** from the liver makes the food alkaline and breaks fats into small globules; the pancreas adds **trypsin** (proteins) and **lipase** (fats); the intestinal wall completes digestion.
5. **Villi**, finger-like projections of the inner lining, give a huge surface for **absorption**; they are richly supplied with blood vessels.
6. **Large intestine:** absorbs more water; the waste leaves through the anus, controlled by the anal sphincter.

blocks.title: Digestive juices at a glance
blocks.body:
| Part | Gland or juice | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Mouth | Salivary glands: saliva (salivary amylase) | starch to sugar |
| Stomach | Gastric glands: hydrochloric acid, pepsin, mucus | acid medium; pepsin digests proteins; mucus protects the lining |
| Small intestine | Liver: bile | makes the food alkaline; breaks fats into small globules (emulsification) |
| Small intestine | Pancreas: pancreatic juice (trypsin, lipase) | trypsin digests proteins; lipase digests emulsified fats |
| Small intestine | Intestinal wall: intestinal juice | proteins to amino acids, carbohydrates to glucose, fats to fatty acids and glycerol |
| Large intestine | – | absorbs water; the rest leaves through the anus |

blocks.question: Which juice makes the food alkaline and breaks fats into small globules?
blocks.explanation: Bile from the liver neutralises the acid from the stomach and emulsifies fats, so that lipase can act on them.
option_feedback: Correct!
Saliva digests starch in the mouth.
Gastric juice is acidic, not alkaline.
It has lipase, which digests fats only after bile has emulsified them.

blocks.title: Releasing energy from food
blocks.body:
In every cell, glucose is first broken down in the **cytoplasm** into **pyruvate**. What happens next depends on oxygen:

- **Anaerobic** (without oxygen), in yeast: pyruvate gives ethanol and carbon dioxide (fermentation). Overall: $\mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} \rightarrow 2C_{2}H_{5}OH + 2CO_{2}}$
- When there is a **lack of oxygen** in our muscle cells (during hard exercise): pyruvate becomes **lactic acid**, which causes cramps. Overall: $\mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} \rightarrow 2C_{3}H_{6}O_{3}}$
- **Aerobic** (with oxygen), in the **mitochondria**: pyruvate is broken down to carbon dioxide and water, releasing much more energy. Overall: $\mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} + 6O_{2} \rightarrow 6CO_{2} + 6H_{2}O}$

The energy released is used to make **ATP**, the energy currency of the cell. Breaking ATP into ADP releases energy for muscle contraction, making proteins, nerve impulses and so on.

blocks.title: Pathways of breakdown of glucose
blocks.body:
| Where | Oxygen | Glucose (6-carbon) is broken down to | Energy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cytoplasm (all cells) | not needed | pyruvate (3-carbon) | a little |
| Yeast (fermentation) | absent | ethanol + carbon dioxide | a little |
| Our muscle cells | lack of oxygen | lactic acid (3-carbon) | a little |
| Mitochondria | present | carbon dioxide + water | a lot |

blocks.title: Breathing in humans
blocks.body:
- Air enters through the **nostrils**; fine hairs and mucus filter it. It passes through the **pharynx** and the **trachea** (wind-pipe), kept open by rings of **cartilage**.
- In the lungs the trachea divides into **bronchi**, then **bronchioles**, which end in balloon-like **alveoli**. The alveoli have very thin walls and an extensive network of blood vessels; spread out, their surface would cover about 80 m².
- **Breathing in:** the ribs are lifted and the **diaphragm** flattens, so the chest cavity becomes larger and air is sucked into the lungs. The lungs always keep some residual air, so there is time for gas exchange.
- **Haemoglobin**, the red pigment in red blood cells, carries oxygen. Carbon dioxide is more soluble in water, so it is mostly carried dissolved in the blood.

Aquatic animals get oxygen dissolved in water, which is far less than in air; so fish breathe much faster than land animals and take in water through the mouth and pass it over the gills.

blocks.question: Where in the cell is pyruvate broken down to carbon dioxide and water?
blocks.explanation: The first step, glucose to pyruvate, happens in the cytoplasm; the aerobic breakdown of pyruvate happens in the mitochondria.
option_feedback: Glucose becomes pyruvate in the cytoplasm; the next step needs mitochondria.
The nucleus controls the cell; it does not respire.
Chloroplasts make food by photosynthesis.
Correct!

blocks.title: Blood, heart and blood vessels
blocks.body:
**Blood** is a fluid connective tissue: **plasma** (carries food, carbon dioxide and nitrogenous waste in dissolved form), **red blood cells** (carry oxygen), **white blood cells** (fight infection) and **platelets** (help blood to clot at a cut).

The **heart** is a muscular pump about the size of a fist, with four chambers:
- **Right side:** receives **deoxygenated** blood from the body in the right atrium and pumps it from the right ventricle to the lungs.
- **Left side:** receives **oxygenated** blood from the lungs in the left atrium and pumps it from the left ventricle to the body.
- **Valves** stop blood flowing backwards. The ventricles have thicker walls than the atria because they pump blood to other organs.

Blood passes through the heart **twice** in one cycle of the body: **double circulation**. Separating oxygenated and deoxygenated blood gives a highly efficient supply of oxygen, which birds and mammals need to keep their body temperature constant.

**Arteries** carry blood away from the heart (thick, elastic walls); **veins** bring it back (thinner walls, valves); **capillaries** are one cell thick and exchange materials with the cells. Normal blood pressure is about 120/80 mm of Hg (systolic/diastolic), measured with a sphygmomanometer.

**Lymph** (tissue fluid) is formed from plasma that escapes through capillary walls into the spaces between cells. It is colourless, has fewer proteins, carries digested and absorbed fat from the intestine, and drains excess fluid back into the blood.

blocks.title: Transport in plants
blocks.body:
- **Xylem** carries water and minerals from the roots to all parts. Root cells take up ions actively, so water moves into the root; as water evaporates from the leaves (**transpiration**), a suction (**transpiration pull**) draws water up. At night, **root pressure** is the main force. Transpiration also helps in temperature regulation.
- **Phloem** carries food (sucrose, amino acids and other substances) from the leaves to other parts, upwards and downwards. This **translocation** uses energy from ATP to load sucrose into the phloem; water then enters by osmosis and the pressure moves the food to where it is needed.

blocks.question: Which chamber of the human heart pumps oxygenated blood to the body?
blocks.explanation: Oxygenated blood from the lungs enters the left atrium and is pumped to the body by the thick-walled left ventricle.
option_feedback: It receives oxygenated blood from the lungs.
It receives deoxygenated blood from the body.
Correct!
It pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

blocks.title: Kidneys and nephrons
blocks.body:
The human excretory system has a pair of **kidneys**, a pair of **ureters**, a **urinary bladder** and a **urethra**. Urine formed in the kidneys flows through the ureters to the bladder, where it is stored until released through the urethra.

Each kidney has many filtering units called **nephrons**:
1. A cluster of thin-walled capillaries, the **glomerulus**, sits in a cup-shaped **Bowman's capsule**. Blood is filtered here.
2. The filtrate passes along the **tubule**. Glucose, amino acids, salts and a major amount of water are **selectively reabsorbed** into the blood.
3. What remains is **urine**, which goes to the collecting duct.

The kidneys filter about 180 L of filtrate a day, but only 1–2 L of urine is made. The amount depends on how much excess water and dissolved waste there is in the body.

If the kidneys fail, an **artificial kidney** removes waste by **dialysis**: blood flows through tubes in a dialysing fluid, and waste diffuses out. Unlike a kidney, it does not reabsorb.

**Plants** get rid of oxygen and excess water through stomata; other wastes are stored in vacuoles or old xylem, removed in falling leaves, stored as gums and resins, or excreted into the soil.

blocks.question: In a nephron, glucose and amino acids are returned to the blood in the:
blocks.explanation: Blood is filtered in the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule; useful substances are reabsorbed along the tubule.
option_feedback: The ureter only carries urine to the bladder.
Correct!
Filtration happens here, not reabsorption.
The bladder only stores urine.

blocks.title: Follow the oxygen, follow the food
blocks.body:
- **Oxygen:** nostrils → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli → blood (haemoglobin) → left side of heart → body cells → mitochondria.
- **Food:** mouth (starch) → stomach (proteins) → small intestine (everything finishes, absorbed by villi) → blood → cells.
- **Waste:** blood → kidney (nephron) → ureter → bladder → urethra.

In the heart: **R**ight = **R**eturns from body, to lungs; **L**eft = from **L**ungs, to body.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
- Writing that respiration means breathing: breathing moves air; respiration releases energy from food in cells.
- Saying that lactic acid forms in yeast: yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide; our muscles make lactic acid.
- Writing that bile is an enzyme: it has no enzymes; it makes the medium alkaline and emulsifies fats.
- Mixing up xylem and phloem: xylem carries water and minerals upwards only; phloem carries food both ways.
- Writing that all arteries carry oxygenated blood: the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

blocks.title: Model it in class
blocks.body: Ask students to blow through a straw into lime water to show carbon dioxide in exhaled air. Use a balloon in a bottle with a rubber sheet as the base to show how the diaphragm moves air. For the heart, draw the four chambers on the floor with chalk and let four students be the blood, walking the double circulation route.

blocks.title: Explain it in your own words
blocks.body: Explain to a friend why a fish breathes faster than a dog, and why the human heart keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood apart.

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **Chapter 4:** carbohydrates, fats and proteins are carbon compounds; respiration is their combustion inside the cell.
- **Chapter 6, Control and Coordination:** nerves and hormones control these processes.
- **Class 11 and 12 Biology:** photosynthesis, respiration and human physiology in detail.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
An athlete runs a 100 m sprint and gets cramps in the leg muscles. A day later, the pain is gone.

(a) What caused the cramps? (b) Why did they go away? (c) Why does the body make this substance and not carbon dioxide during the sprint?

**Answer:** (a) During the sprint the muscles did not get enough oxygen, so pyruvate was converted to **lactic acid**: $\mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} \rightarrow 2C_{3}H_{6}O_{3}}$ Its build-up causes cramps. (b) With rest and enough oxygen, the lactic acid is carried away by the blood and broken down. (c) The aerobic pathway in the mitochondria needs oxygen, which was not supplied fast enough; the anaerobic pathway still gives a little energy quickly.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- Life processes are nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion.
- Autotrophs make food by photosynthesis; heterotrophs take in food made by others.
- In humans, digestion starts in the mouth (starch), continues in the stomach (proteins) and finishes in the small intestine, where villi absorb the food.
- Glucose is broken down to pyruvate in the cytoplasm, then to carbon dioxide and water in the mitochondria (aerobic), or to ethanol or lactic acid without enough oxygen; the energy is stored as ATP.
- Blood, a four-chambered heart and blood vessels give double circulation; lymph returns fluid to the blood. In plants, xylem carries water and phloem carries food.
- Nephrons in the kidneys filter blood and make urine; plants remove waste through stomata, leaves, vacuoles, gums and resins.

blocks.title: Board exam tips
blocks.body:
- Practise labelled diagrams: human digestive system, respiratory system, heart (sectional view), nephron, stomata (open and closed), and nutrition in amoeba.
- Learn the three pathways of breakdown of glucose as a flow chart, with where each happens.
- Name the enzyme, its gland and its substrate together: salivary amylase (starch), pepsin (proteins), trypsin (proteins), lipase (fats).
- In difference questions (xylem/phloem, aerobic/anaerobic, artery/vein), write the points in a two-column table.

blocks.front: Basic filtering unit of the kidney

blocks.back: Blood passes through the heart twice in one complete cycle of the body: once to the lungs and once to the rest of the body.
